item.title: Is the "Addictive Personality" Real?
item.description:
Personality

Is the "Addictive Personality" Real?

Can you have an "addictive personality"? Yes and no. Here are the facts.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Two million-person studies found shared addiction risk and personality–substance links.
  • There is no single addictive personality. Multiple traits create multiple pathways to addiction.
  • Some people seek stimulation. Others seek relief. Repeated exposure can overwhelm either pathway.
  • Risk is not destiny. Treat the person and the pathway—not a supposedly defective personality.

Two enormous genetic studies have reopened one of addiction psychiatry’s oldest debates: Is the "addictive personality" a valid concept?

In September 2026, Ted Schwaba and colleagues analyzed the genetics of the Big Five personality traits in 1.14 million people. They identified 1,260 associated genetic variants, including 824 that had not been reported before. Some genetic signals overlapped with substance use. Genetic liability to conscientiousness was correlated with less substance use across substances. Higher neuroticism was linked with several substance outcomes, especially alcohol dependence. Higher agreeableness was generally protective against addiction.

Three years earlier, Alexander Hatoum and more than 150 colleagues analyzed data from over 1.1 million people. They found a general addiction risk factor spanning problematic alcohol and tobacco use, cannabis use disorder, and opioid use disorder. They also found substance-specific risks. Shared vulnerability, yes. One addiction gene, no.

Put the studies together, and the answer seems new, exciting, and strangely familiar: Personality matters. So do genes. But neither study gives us a test capable of identifying those who will become addicted.

Genome-wide association studies detect patterns across populations. They don’t read any single individual's mind. A polygenic score is not a diagnosis and it certainly is no crystal ball. It is also not equally accurate across ancestries.

Three Thousand Years of Addiction Explanations

For three millennia, people have tried to explain why some lose control while others do not. The data was dwarfed by the ever-changing explanations.

Ancient Western traditions emphasized excess, wisdom, character, reason, or self-command. Early Buddhist thought emphasized something different: craving and attachment as universal human processes—not evidence of a defective class of people. Aristotle called acting against one’s better judgment akrasia. Benjamin Rush later moved habitual drunkenness away from simple sin and toward disease and loss of control

History of Addictive Personality
Source: Mark Gold, MD

In an 1897 letter to Wilhelm Fliess, Freud called masturbation the “primal addiction” and viewed alcohol, morphine, and tobacco as substitutes. In that same letter, however, he wondered whether addiction was curable—or whether “analysis and therapy must come to a halt.”

In 1933, psychoanalyst Sándor Radó published his famous paper calling addiction “pharmacothymia,” or a chemical shortcut for changing a painful mood. The word has disappeared, but the observation has not. People do not always take drugs to feel good. Often, they take them to stop feeling bad.

The Alcoholic Personality Problem

Then emerged the search for the alcoholic personality. Some patients were said to be primarily impulsive, sensation-seeking, and antisocial. Others were anxious, inhibited, depressed, or compulsive. Some appeared quite ordinary until alcohol reorganized their lives. Yet all supposedly shared one personality. This was convenient. Also, circular: People drank because they had an alcoholic personality. How did we know? They drank.

Jellinek’s disease model recognized that different people travel different roads to the same disorder. For alcoholism, Cloninger later proposed an earlier-onset, more heritable and externalizing pathway and a later-onset, anxious and harm-avoidant pathway.

In this tradition, Harvard’s Edward Khantzian made the relief pathway clinically useful. His self-medication hypothesis asked a better question: Why does this drug fit this person? Opioids may quiet rage or dysphoria. Stimulants may temporarily provide energy, confidence, or focus. Alcohol and benzodiazepines may reduce worrying or hyperarousal. The drug then becomes a crude prescription—fast, effective, and eventually destructive. The attempted solution becomes the disease. Ken Blum’s reward deficiency syndrome asked why ordinary rewards may not be rewarding enough.

What the Genetics Changes

Epidemiological studies tell us that about half the risk for addiction is genetic; vulnerability seems to be roughly the same for all drugs. A 50 percent genetic risk is higher than for type II diabetes or hypertension, which we often think of as genetic diseases.

Sensation seeking or reward deficiency may open the door. Anxiety, anhedonia, ADHD, trauma, or insomnia may influence the drug of choice. Then repeated use, potency, and brain adaptation may overwhelm the original vulnerabilities. Genes may influence vulnerability, but exposure remains required: No first use or exposure, no addiction.

The new genetics replaces a pejorative label with multiple pathways to risk.

Who experiments? Who finds a particular drug unusually useful? Who, after repeated exposure, cannot stop? No single trait answers all three questions.

Old AA wisdom said alcoholism “skipped a generation.” Genes do not skip generations, but the child of an alcoholic may have seen way too much, and so avoided alcohol entirely. The vulnerability may have remained, but without use, alcohol was never a problem. A grandchild who drank could make the family history appear to skip a generation: Genes were transmitted, but exposure was not.

Higher neuroticism may increase interest in drugs promising relief. Lower conscientiousness may make planning, delaying gratification, and resisting immediate reward harder. Higher conscientiousness and agreeableness may offer some protection. May, not must.

Personality can influence experimentation, drug choice, and stopping. But personality before addiction should not be confused with behavior during intoxication, withdrawal, craving, or desperation. Someone lying to obtain heroin is not necessarily a dishonest person. Heroin dependence can make honesty extraordinarily expensive.

The drug matters too. Fentanyl can addict anyone, even a careful anesthesiologist. Alcohol can trap a conscientious physician. Cocaine can overwhelm a successful, motivated person. Potency, availability, age at first exposure, trauma, psychiatric illness, peers, and brain adaptation all matter.

Personality is part of the story. It is not the whole story.

Why This Matters Today

The addictive personality label survives because it is simple. It turns risk into identity. It also suggests that people with addiction are defective—and safely different from the rest of us.

The genetics tells a less comfortable—and more democratic—story. Risk is spread across the population, shared partly across drugs, and changed by development and exposure.

Risk is not destiny, and behavior in the middle of addiction should not become a lifetime description of a person.

This changes treatment: Do not treat a mythical addictive personality. Treat the pathway to addiction and treat the individual.

A sensation-seeking adolescent may need structure, alternative rewards, and reduced drug access. A traumatized patient using opioids for emotional anesthesia needs evidence-based addiction treatment and trauma-informed care. ADHD, depression, anxiety, and insomnia need treatment—not dismissal as excuses. Patients whose lives have narrowed to drug reward need medication, recovery support, and help rebuilding ordinary rewards.

Prevention should follow the same logic. Delay first exposure to substances. Reduce access to potent drugs. Treat psychiatric illness early. Strengthen families and schools. Genetics may eventually sharpen prevention. Today, it already teaches humility.

So, is there one addictive personality? No. There is no single defective personality shared by everyone with addiction. Instead, multiple partly heritable traits alter risk through different pathways—and then there is the drug, the dose, the environment, and time.

That answer is less catchy than “the addictive personality.” It is also more accurate, less stigmatizing, and far more useful.

item.title: Am I Addicted to Football?
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Am I Addicted to Football?

3 things that make the beautiful game so compelling.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Football fandom is not a recognized behavioral addiction, but some research suggests it could be.
  • Football's scarcity of goals and unpredictable results keep fans hooked waiting for rewards.
  • The near-miss effect keeps gamblers, and many fans, fixated on potential wins.

‘I’m never watching them again,’ I say to my wife, collapsing into bed after a Monday night defeat.

‘Hmmm,’ my wife says, turning a page of her book.

'I’m serious this time,” I say. ‘Don’t let me do it. I’m sick and tired of this. It just makes me miserable.’

My wife strokes my shoulder. ‘If you’re serious, we could do something nice on Saturday – visit some antiques shops in Burwash?’

‘Yes,’ I say. ‘I’m completely up for that. Just don’t let me watch. Please.’

Tuesday arrives, and I am doing brilliantly. Football is dead to me. I am a man reborn. Sky Sports remains untouched. Champions League fixtures pass me by like clouds in the sky.

Wednesday and Thursday are the same. No league table checking.

On Friday, my wife reminds me about our Burwash trip.

‘Absolutely,’ I declare. ‘No game for me this weekend. I’ve moved on.’

But then Saturday morning arrives.

At 3pm, instead of strolling around Burwash, I’m in my swivel chair in my office – watching Wolves lose on a dodgy stick.

What has happened to me? Am I addicted to football?

I do some research.

I start by checking to see whether football fandom appears in the DSM-5 or ICD-11. Nothing. There are few official behavioral addictions, and football addiction is not one of them.

But at least one psychiatrist argues that football fandom might qualify as a behavioural addiction

Psychiatrist Massimo Lanzaro lays out the DSM criteria for behavioural addictions and matches them, symptom by symptom, to some football fans.

  • Repetitive engagement leading to dysfunction
  • Obsession, withdrawal, cravings
  • Failed attempts to stop
  • Neglect of other life domains
  • Continued use despite harm
  • Risking relationships

The symptoms sounded suspiciously familiar.

Next, I speak to Professor Adam Alter of NYU, a best-selling author on behavioural addictions. From him, I learn that there were four reasons I was doomed to miss my trip to Burwash. Together, they hack into the brain’s reward systems like a slot machine.

The first is the scarcity of goals.

In football, goals are rare things, unlike in cricket or rugby, where the scoreboard is ticking over all the time. And when something is limited in supply, people tend to value it more. Marketers exploit the scarcity principle to sell us their products all the time; limited offers like ‘only two left in stock’ and 24-hour flash sales.

Research shows that when people are presented with jars – one full to the brim with chocolate cookies and the other with just a couple left inside, they rate the cookies in the emptier jar as tastier, even though the biscuits are identical.

Scientists have shown how powerful this scarcity effect is in the brains of football fans, too. Nine Glasgow Rangers supporters were put into brain scanners and shown four-second clips of their team either scoring, narrowly missing or just passing the ball harmlessly in midfield. When Rangers scored, the researchers saw an ‘intense pleasure response’ in the anterior cingulate cortex – akin to cocaine use.

The second factor is the unpredictability of results. You only have to look at the opening games of this season; Hull beating Man United, for example. Last year Macclesfield beat FA Cup holders Crystal Palace.

In a study by Gregory Berns and colleagues, participants lay in brain scanners while receiving squirts of juice and water through tubes in their mouths. In one condition, the water and juice were delivered in a predictable sequence. In the other, the order was chaotic. The participants said they preferred the juice but didn’t care about the sequence. Their brains told a different story. Dopamine-linked reward regions responded far more strongly when the drinks arrived unpredictably. The juice tasted better. But the surprise was more exciting. Slot machines work the same way. Most spins, you lose. But every so often – bang – three cherries, and your reward circuits light up.

Psychologists call this a variable ratio schedule – rewards delivered after an unpredictable number of actions. It is the most powerful form of reinforcement we know. Our ancestors were rewarded for testing out new, unpredictable, territories to maximise resources.

Football exploits our predilection for variability mercilessly.

The third factor is the ‘near-miss effect’.

Gambling companies know all about this one too. Scratchcards and slot machines leave you one symbol away from a payout all the time. The flicker of maybe next time keeps the dopamine flowing. Football gives you so many ‘near misses’ that you are in a constant state of anticipation.

In the Rangers fan study, where brain reward centres lit up after a goal, the researchers discovered that another part of the brain – the putamen — lit up when there was a “near miss”. The putamen, the researchers argue, plays a crucial role in anticipating emotional events.

Football’s compelling magic lies in the tease of what might happen, not just in what does. The brain has to reward the wanting; otherwise desire would simply switch itself off whenever resources – or goals – are scarce.

The final reason has nothing to do with football itself. It has to do with what Alter describes as the ‘delivery device’. It’s football’s equivalent of a crack pipe – the smartphone.

In the olden days, I’d be depressed for a bit after going to a game or watching Match of the Day, but then that would be it. There’d be no reminders until Saint & Greavsie the following Saturday lunchtime. Now there’s no getting away, even though I live in Hastings, far from Molineux stadium. There are pings, reruns and nonstop stats fed through the screen like intravenous drips.

The cues are everywhere, impossible to avoid. It’s like being a recovering heroin addict and seeing billboards for needles and smack on every street corner.

Which might explain why, after 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 games without a win – after swearing I’ll never watch again – I’m still watching.

And I’m not going to Burwash.

Learn more from my new book, Till I Die: Why Football Means Everything (Even When It Shouldn’t).

item.title: Could GLP-1 Medications Quiet the Urge Behind BFRBs?
item.description:
Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors

Could GLP-1 Medications Quiet the Urge Behind BFRBs?

Case reports suggest GLP-1s may reduce many compulsive urges.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1 meds may reduce urges behind body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs).
  • Case reports suggest GLP-1s "quiet" urges like hair pulling, akin to reducing "food noise."
  • Treating the whole person with a broad view and integrative approach is essential to improving BFRBs.

Ask almost anyone about GLP-1 medications right now, and you'll get a lively conversation—not just about weight, but about everything else these drugs seem to potentially impact. One of the more surprising conversations in therapist circles involves a set of behaviors most of us don't connect to metabolism at all: body-focused repetitive behaviors, or BFRBs.

BFRBs include hair pulling, skin picking, nail biting, and related behaviors like cheek biting, lip biting, and cuticle picking. What these behaviors tend to share is a certain tenacity. They often persist despite distress and repeated, earnest attempts to stop.

Potential Impact of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on BFRBs

What makes GLP-1 receptor agonists, namely semaglutide, tirzepatide, and others, so interesting is that their effects appear to extend well beyond appetite. GLP-1 receptors are found throughout the brain, including in regions tied to reward and impulse control. And, there is emerging evidence that these medications may quiet what we consider to be the brain's "craving" circuitry: the urge-driven, automatic pull that shows up not only in overeating, but in drinking, smoking, and, as case reports suggest, might also be in BFRBs as well.

While we don’t yet have sufficient, controlled research on GLP-1s and BFRBs, we have case reports from both patients and clinicians suggesting there may be a relationship, and these reports have been consistent enough to warrant attention. Patients have reported that these medications, prescribed for weight management, have stopped or sharply reduced their hair pulling, skin picking, or nail biting. Others describe the urge itself as having "quieted." Perhaps the “food noise” often associated with these medications may also be “BFRB noise.” This is notable, given how resistant these behaviors can be to change.

It is possible these medications are modulating the same reward and urge pathways that underlie BFRBs, essentially turning down the signal strength of the behavior loop. Whether that's a direct neurochemical effect, an indirect one through reduced overall impulsivity/compulsivity, or something we have yet to identify, we don’t yet know. But it’s a question worth exploring.

It is important to consider this in the context of BFRB heterogeneity: Even if this holds true, it may describe the experience of only a subset of people living with a BFRB. If GLP-1s offer some people relief from urges they've wrestled with for years, this is significant. It may even be a clue, pointing us toward better, more integrative approaches to treatment.

Role of Behavioral Therapy in BFRB Treatment

Of course, although this is an exciting avenue to explore, it’s also important to remember that behavioral therapy remains the standard of care for BFRBs, and it does something medication cannot do—it addresses the function the behavior serves, the reason it shows up there in the first place, and helps to more adaptively meet that need. Ultimately, treating the whole person with a broad view and integrative approach to treatment is essential to improving outcomes.

item.title: When "I Can't" Means "I Won't"
item.description:
Motivation

When "I Can't" Means "I Won't"

Changing a few familiar words can restore your sense of agency.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • "I can't" can turn a choice into an impossibility, while "I won't" names the real decision you are making.
  • "I'll try" can preserve an exit before you even begin; "I will" asks you to commit, even when you are unsure.
  • Not every "can't" is a disguised "won't." Real constraints deserve to be named honestly.
Yoda Cave
Source: Iceland Travel Tips

"'I can't' means 'I won't.'"

That was my father's answer, every time, when I told him I couldn't do something as a child. I didn't understand it then. I only knew it frustrated me, because I wasn't trying to make a philosophical point. I was trying to explain that something felt too hard, too uncomfortable, or simply beyond me.

He wouldn't let me confuse reluctance with impossibility.

I live by that sentence now. It surfaced again recently on Iceland's south coast, in a cave called Gígjagjá, better known as the Yoda Cave for the shape its opening cuts into the sky. Standing there, I thought of Yoda's own version: "Do. Or do not. There is no try." Long before I knew who Yoda was, I had my own at home.

"I can't" closes a door before you've looked through it

I can't take a real break. I can't speak up in that meeting.

These sound like facts. Often, they are decisions we haven't owned yet.

"I can't" places something outside our control. If it is impossible, there is nothing left to examine, so we stop looking. Over time, that language can leave us feeling stuck or resentful of circumstances we may have had some hand in creating.

"I won't" is less comfortable because it hands the choice back. Say, "I won't speak up in that meeting," and a real question follows: Why not? Maybe you are afraid of how it will land. Maybe you want to be seen as easy to work with. None of those answers makes you weak. But a decision can be examined and changed. An impossibility just sits there.

"I won't" is not an accusation. Sometimes it is the clearest and healthiest boundary available to us. The power is in recognizing it as a choice rather than disguising it as something outside our control.

"I'll try" can keep one foot near the exit

"I'll try" can sound like commitment while quietly keeping an escape in view. "I will" asks something more of us. It does not guarantee success, but it does ask us to engage fully.

"I will have the conversation" moves you toward it. "I'll try to find the right time" can keep you circling it indefinitely.

My father never said, "'I'll try' means 'I won't.'" He didn't need to. Once you hear, "'I can't' means 'I won't'" often enough, you start catching its cousins on your own.

Some things really are impossible, and that is worth saying honestly, too

There are caregiving responsibilities and illnesses no choice of words can remove. When one of those is true, naming it plainly is not a failure of will.

The useful question is not whether "can't" is ever allowed. It is whether the obstacle is truly immovable, or whether doing the thing would require a risk, cost, or discomfort you are not willing to accept.

That distinction matters. If the constraint is real, you can stop arguing with yourself about it. If the issue is the tradeoff, you have something to weigh: the cost and whether it's worth paying. You may still choose not to pay it. That doesn't make the choice smaller. It makes it visible.

Agency is not measured by constant action. Sometimes "I won't" is exactly the right answer, whether that means turning down one more obligation, or choosing instead to rest, wait, or protect what matters most.

What matters is knowing the difference.

The words we inherit keep shaping us

"Do or do not. There is no try."
Source: Laura Berger

I've written before that words are worlds, that what we say builds us up or wears us down. I meant it about the mantras we choose deliberately. What I understand better now is that the sentences shaping us often aren't chosen at all. They are handed to us early, by someone who cared enough to interrupt us.

This week, catch yourself saying "I can't" or "I'll try." Before correcting it, ask what it might be protecting. Then say the other version out loud: "I won't" or "I will." Notice what shows up. Relief, resistance, fear, clarity. Whatever it is, that is useful information.

My father is 83 now, and if I called him today and told him I couldn't do something, I already know what he'd say.

item.title: Financial Abuse Is Emotional Abuse
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

Financial Abuse Is Emotional Abuse

This is a form of control you should never ignore.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Financial abuse is often subtle, leaving no visible scars but deeply impacting victims.
  • Signs of financial abuse include exclusion from decisions and creating debt without consent.
  • Confronting financial abuse requires open communication and possibly a counselor.

In my last post, I discussed the differences between financial infidelity and financial abuse. These terms might seem interchangeable, but they are not.

As I see both of these issues in my family law practice, I want to delve a little deeper into “financial abuse,” as it is the more nefarious version of the two.

When people think about “abuse” in a relationship, it is easy to picture physical violence, yelling, threats, or other kinds of emotional manipulation. But I have found that one of the most damaging forms of abuse can be much harder to recognize—because it is harder for the victim to recognize—and often leaves no visible scars.

What Is Financial Abuse, Exactly?

Financial abuse is rooted in a need for control. One partner will use family finances or access to money to gain power over the other person. If you have a relationship with a person where you share finances, it can happen. Most of the time it happens gradually, which sometimes makes it difficult for the victim to recognize what is going on.

As you might imagine, it happens in marriages and, as I have seen firsthand, can get worse during a separation and before and after a divorce.

I have worked with many clients as a divorce attorney who told me they just were not good with finances or had always depended on their spouse to handle issues with money. In some cases, over time, they realized they were actually cut out of financial decision-making for the family.

It is important to distinguish this aspect of financial abuse from a couple that has naturally divided their roles and responsibilities.

One person may enjoy managing investments and handling the day-to-day bookkeeping of paying bills while the other handles childcare, cooking, or running the household. Or, as we have seen, there are just about as many combinations of dividing labor as there are couples.

Those arrangements are not inherently problematic—as long as both partners have access to information, understand the family's financial picture, and can participate in major decisions.

The warning signs emerge when there is not full transparency and what was framed as “financial management” is actually “financial control.”

Red Flags of Financial Abuse

Here are a few red flags that your partner’s “financial management” might have crossed the line into “financial abuse”:

  • Restricting access to money. A controlling partner may refuse to allow the other spouse access to bank accounts, credit cards, passwords, or financial records. This can even include providing an "allowance" that is closely monitored.
  • Excluding a partner from financial decision-making. One spouse may purchase property, take out loans, refinance a home, or make significant investments without discussing the decisions. First, this is not a good idea for keeping a marriage healthy; also, the excluded partner loses both knowledge and confidence regarding the family's finances over time.
  • Sabotaging a person's ability to become financially independent. In some cases, a partner may discourage or, in extreme cases, forbid employment. This could include interfering with educational opportunities or insisting that the other spouse leave a promising career. Note: This is different from when couples jointly decide that one parent will stay home with children, as that decision is made collaboratively—not imposed through intimidation or coercion.
  • Creating debt in a partner's name. This is another way a partner might use control over access to accounts. This typically happens without the partner knowing what is happening, which makes it even worse.
  • Other forms of deception. Hiding assets, refusing to pay agreed-upon household expenses despite having the resources to do so, or intentionally damaging the other person's credit are other ways a partner can control the finances and potentially affect their credit score and future capacity to get loans, become financially independent, etc.

As I have seen many times, these behaviors sometimes escalate in divorce, with one spouse attempting to conceal income, delay support payments, or use litigation costs as leverage to force an unfavorable settlement.

Remember: Financial Abuse Is Emotional Abuse

Financial abuse is often difficult to identify because it typically coexists with emotional manipulation. Eroding the victim’s self-confidence on all types of issues is the goal, and in the case of financial abuse, it starts to make the victim doubt they can handle their own finances. This, in turn, can make it very hard to leave an unhealthy relationship.

How to Take Action

It should be noted that if you recognize some of these patterns in your own relationship, it does not mean your marriage is beyond repair. If you raise it with your partner and have a good, honest conversation, you can restore the balance. (An external counselor can help with this, too.)

However, if any of these points is also accompanied by intimidation, threats, isolation, or other forms of abuse, it is important to take the situation seriously.

I would recommend finding trusted professionals to talk it through first. But other actions you might take include:

  • Documenting financial information
  • Making copies of important records
  • Finding out what your assets and debts are and where they are held
  • Establishing your own credit if possible

I have heard: "I don't even know what questions to ask." That uncertainty is the goal if the partner intends to keep you in the dark, as financial abuse is designed to leave people feeling powerless.

And as I always say, please take care of yourself and your children during what can be a very stressful time.

item.title: Learning From the Drucker-Like Figures of Psychology
item.description:
Career

Learning From the Drucker-Like Figures of Psychology

Exploring insights from boundary-spanning psychologists.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, Albert Bandura, and Edgar H. Schein enjoyed Drucker-like careers.
  • Csikszentmihalyi was known for flow, Bandura for self-efficacy, and Schein for psychological safety and more.
  • Each worked at the high levels and contributed intellectually long past traditional retirement age.
Source: dizain / Shutterstock

I’m always looking to identify and learn from people who, in their own fields, were comparable to Peter Drucker, the father of modern management, who died at 95 in 2005. My criteria are for people who have operated at the highest and most accomplished levels in their field, lived to an advanced age, and contributed intellectually well past traditional retirement age.

Three psychologists who fit this Drucker-like criteria passed away in recent years: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, at 87 in 2021; Albert Bandura, at 95 that same year; and Edgar H. Schein, at 94 in 2023. What they researched, taught, and wrote about during their lengthy careers is congruent with and complementary to Drucker’s work.

Peter Drucker’s Achievements

First, to briefly recap an extraordinary life and career: Drucker wrote nearly 40 books on management and other subjects, and was the first, in the late 1950s, to identify a class of knowledge workers. He was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest honor for civilians, at age 92, and taught at an institution that was eventually named for him, the Drucker School of Management, at Claremont Graduate University, in Claremont, California. His work is further carried on at a related organization based at the university, The Drucker Institute, as well as the Global Peter Drucker Forum, in his native Vienna, Austria.

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi: Flow

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi, after a long career at the University of Chicago, began teaching in Claremont in 1999, initially at the Drucker School, where I interviewed him in 2005. I was impressed by his affable and generous nature.

Csikszentmihalyi was a co-founder of the field of positive psychology. His best-known book, Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience, was published in 1990. In 2003, I reviewed his book Good Business: Leadership, Flow and the Making of Meaning for USA TODAY. In the context of that book, I described the concept of flow as: “being so absorbed in an activity that we shut out distractions and worries to devote all our energy to the task at hand. It can occur in work or play, but the focus here is how people can find flow when they work, and how leaders can encourage flow in employees.”

Albert Bandura: Self-Efficacy

Albert Bandura was a renowned psychology professor at Stanford University whose influence extended to other domains, including the business world. As knowledge workers face mounting anxiety about the current and future effects of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on their work and livelihoods, calling on Bandura’s seminal concept of self-efficacy can be helpful.

Self-efficacy, which I wrote about in Create Your Future the Peter Drucker Way, goes beyond confidence, though it is related to it. It falls within Bandura’s social cognitive theory. If we have self-efficacy, we believe that we can take on a task and be successful. Bandura explained that this concept builds on a series of successes, “personal mastery,” which we can apply or use as motivation elsewhere. It won’t just happen out of nowhere; it requires perseverance, grit, and resilience.

Edgar H. Schein: Psychological Safety

As he was a psychologist, teacher, consultant, and author, the work of Edgar H. Schein is a common factor among several of the most important topics within organizations today: psychological safety, organizational culture, and humility. He was a longtime MIT Sloan School of Management professor whose books, such as Organizational Culture and Leadership and Humble Inquiry, reached wide audiences, particularly in the business world.

Psychological safety, in particular, has become one of the most referenced concepts in organizations—business and otherwise. One of the best-known experts in the field is Harvard Business School professor Amy C. Edmondson. Schein wrote the foreword for her book Teaming, in which she writes of the concept’s long roots: “In 1965, MIT professors Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis (later a professor at the University of Southern California), discussed the need to create psychological safety to make people feel secure and capable of changing.”

Becoming American

In an age of worldwide anxiety about immigration, it’s worth pointing out that Drucker, Csikszentmihalyi, Schein, and Bandura were all born outside the United States, came here as young adults, and built their careers at universities in this country. Schein even wrote a memoir about his immigrant experience, Becoming American: My First Learning Journey.

Human Achievement

Drucker, Csikszentmihalyi, Bandura, and Schein are great examples of what is possible in human achievement, including the rewards of long, fruitful careers; professional experimentation; and reaching out beyond disciplines to different audiences. They exemplify the value of teaching and connecting with students while remaining lifelong learners. And their work transcended their own disciplines to have effects in other domains. They personified productive longevity—in their cases, teaching, researching, writing, consulting, and creating for the benefit of the greater good until shortly before their deaths.

Each slowly and deliberately built careers based on hard work, ingenuity, creativity, and curiosity. At this inflection point in history, even if we do not reach the heights they achieved, there is nothing stopping us from building our careers in similar ways

item.title: What Sounded Like Harsh Parenting Was Really an Act of Love
item.description:
Parenting

What Sounded Like Harsh Parenting Was Really an Act of Love

Tayler's story shows how boundaries can transform reactive behavior.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • What kids need most when they're spiraling out of control are parents who can be calm and keep them safe.
  • Being able to set the appropriate boundary and the support the child's needs in explosive moments is key.
  • Separating briefly while keeping the child safe can prevent reinforcement of tantrums.

Tayler, 5, flips out at a restaurant because her little sister, Stella, is sitting next to Mom. Tayler starts screeching and pushing Stella out of the chair. Her parents, Andrew and Lizzy, can’t get her back in control. The more they try to reason and problem-solve with her, or offer calming tools, the more escalated she becomes. (Dad calls this Tayler’s “street fighter” mode.)

In situations like this, Lizzy and Andrew often acquiesce to whatever demand Tayler is making to head off the inevitable explosion, especially in a public place. Stella also often gives Tayler what she wants, pacifying her sister to keep the peace.

Lizzy and Andrew are very concerned about this dynamic for several reasons:

  • It’s enabling Tayler to think she can always get her way, and that ruling through intimidation and threats works.
  • Tayler isn’t learning to accept and cope with limits.
  • Tayler is sucking all the oxygen out of the family, and they are having very negative feelings about her.
  • Stella is learning to be a pleaser and to forgo her own needs to prevent Tayler’s tantrums.

Andrew, Lizzy, and I have been working on an approach that enables them to stay calm and in control, while holding boundaries to help Tayler learn to be more flexible and accept limits.

Our Solution

This is what we came up with:

The next time they are going to a restaurant, they explain to Tayler that in public places, there are rules to keep everyone in that space safe and comfortable, just like the teachers do at school. In restaurants, this means sitting at the table, using inside voices, and safe bodies. If she has a hard time doing this, Mom/Dad will be helpers and take her to a quiet space to give her a chance to calm so she can return to the table—the goal.

They have to enact the plan just a few weeks later. The trigger is Tayler’s insistence that Stella’s helping of ice cream is bigger. She demands Stella give her some of her portion. Lizzy tries to reason with her. Tayler—in red zone, processing nothing— storms over to Stella and starts aggressively digging her spoon into Stella’s bowl. No strategy is working to get her to stop.

Andrew steps in. He simply says, “I’ll be your helper” (the less language the better) as he guides Tayler away from the table and moves her to the car. He puts on her favorite music, hoping this will calm her, but she starts attacking him—hitting and scratching. She is so dysregulated that he can’t get her buckled safely into her seat. Realizing he is a stimulus—his presence is harmful, not helpful—he tells Tayler he’ll wait right outside the car; when she’s calm, they can return to the table.

In less than five minutes—when Tayler sees that kicking and screaming at the window is not getting a reaction, and that dad is still calmly standing aside the car—she calms. Andrew refrains from any lesson-teaching. He just gives her a big hug. They return to the restaurant; Tayler eats her ice cream (Lizzy had asked the waiter to put it back in the freezer!). Tayler is a delight the remainder of the night.

Note that I hear stories like this frequently from parents: When they hold a limit calmly, their children are noticeably more content and connected once the storm passes. As uncomfortable as it is for these parents to have to take such seemingly extreme measures, they had given their child exactly what they needed, which enabled the child to move on in a positive way.

The Take-Home: Don't Judge an Intervention by Its Cover

It’s all in how it’s implemented. In this case, the parent didn’t shame, berate, reject, or abandon his child. He was calm, connected, validating of her difficult feelings, and showed that he could be her rock—do what it takes to prevent her from being destructive—and help her get back to a place where she could rejoin the family and feel good about herself.

What a gift.

If you’re still feeling uncomfortable about this approach, I encourage you to ask yourself the following question: What are the alternatives, and the potential outcomes/lessons learned from those alternatives?

  • The whole family has to leave the restaurant. (The child controls the family; the sibling grows resentful of the big reactor.)
  • You give in to what the child is demanding (reinforcing a very unhealthy dynamic and increasing your child’s inflexibility and sense of entitlement).
  • You stay in whatever safe space you’ve taken your child to and let them beat up on you, fearing that if you separate yourself, you’re abandoning them (an unfortunate and ultimately harmful message from influencers skewing and sending false messages about “gentle parenting.”) What parent can stay calm—exactly what children need from their moms and dads when they are spiraling—when the parent is not able to get their child in control and is being physically attacked?

When I started in this field of practice, I never imagined I'd be advising parents to physically secure their child in a car and not stay in the car with them. Then I began working in the trenches with big reactors. Every day I was hearing stories and receiving recordings of parents and children completely out of control, with no clear boundary to keep either of them safe.

Most mental health specialists agree that what children need is a calm, connected, warm, loving, and sturdy parent—a mental and physical state that is impossible to sustain while feeling out of control and under attack by one's own child.

I share these stories from the trenches, not as a panacea, or “the approach” for this kind of situation for all children. There is never a one-size-fits-all solution. Not to mention that sometimes (and often, with big reactors) what sounds good in theory fails in practice. (Most parents who come to see me have tried myriad strategies to get their kids to calm—taking deep breaths, offering a bear hug or other forms of comfort, using "if/then"—but find their kids are in the red zone and are unable to engage in or accept any calming strategies.)

I share these stories to illustrate the importance of finding the right boundary together with the “just-right” support and scaffolding your child needs in that difficult moment to be safe and to regulate. Indeed, in this kind of situation, some families may decide to just never go to a restaurant, and that may be the right decision based on their child's coping capacities. What we don't want is for parents to lower expectations when—with the right boundary and support—the child could work it through and learn to manage in difficult situations.

item.title: The Dolly Parton Effect: Why Celebrity Loss Feels Personal
item.description:
Parasocial Relationships

The Dolly Parton Effect: Why Celebrity Loss Feels Personal

When a celebrity dies, we mourn more than a person; we mourn a piece of ourselves.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Parasocial bonds can make the loss of a celebrity feel deeply personal.
  • Celebrity deaths often reconnect us with memories and past chapters in our lives.
  • Healing can begin through shared rituals and carrying a legacy forward.

Do you remember where you were when you learned that Dolly Parton had died? I was in a meeting, and a person looked up from their phone and shared that they’d just seen the headline that Dolly was gone. We all paused our discussion as the weight of the news landed on each of us. For a moment, the room felt different. We realized that millions of people were hearing the same news and experiencing the same sense of loss. We were mourning the loss of someone we only knew by her deeds and her reputation, not as a personal friend. Yet the grief over the loss was genuine.

It’s not unusual to see a major headline or hear a news story about the death of an icon and feel like you’ve lost someone close to you. It can be confusing, though, to suddenly find yourself tearing up over news like this—whether you’re alone in private or among others in public. Some of us might even be ashamed of our strong emotional reaction to this type of event.

“Why Am I Crying Over a Stranger?”

There’s a clear explanation for our sometimes expected, sometimes surprising, reactions to the loss or critical illness of a public figure. We are experiencing something called parasocial mourning. This phenomenon is actually a deeply human, neurobiological response to the loss of a shared anchor of our cultural identity.

The Science Behind Subjective Closeness

The term parasocial relationship describes the one-sided relationships that we have with media figures. While we may never meet a public figure in real life, we feel connected to them due to the amount of information about their lives that we take in through the media. Parasocial relationships can be good for us in a variety of ways (Hoffner & Bond, 2022). They can be health-promoting by improving health-related behaviors, by destigmatizing mental health issues, and by providing a sense of connection to that person as well as to others who feel a similar appreciation and admiration for them.

Research shows that the level of closeness we feel to a celebrity helps determine the intensity of grief we feel at their loss (Baker & Cohen, 2024). When we tear up when we hear a Dolly song now, it’s not because we’re feeling the loss of a talented singer/songwriter. It’s because we’ve lost someone whose presence in our lives carried significance and meaning, even if we hadn’t consciously appreciated that at the time.

Baker and Cohen (2024) explained that our brains process grief based on subjective closeness to someone who’s passed, not physical proximity. When a celebrity’s music, philanthropy, or TV or movie roles accompany us through different chapters of our lives, their loss can feel deeply personal. Over time, they are woven into the fabric of our memories and identities. Dolly was an icon, known not only for her exceptional musical talent but also for her generosity toward others. She was legendary for promoting literacy, supporting medical advances, and helping families stay afloat financially when disaster struck. We aren’t grieving just the person but also the sense of familiarity and comfort they represented.

We’ve Lost a Chapter of Our Own Lives

The loss of a celebrity is felt as a personal loss of part of ourselves. We aren’t just mourning the person; we are mourning who we were when their presence in our lives began. For instance, certain songs can take us back to an earlier point in our lives and make us a little nostalgic. When a person who created that music or starred in that show we loved as teens or represented glamour and beauty at a time when we needed that most—think Princess Diana—passes away, we experience the closing of a piece of our own history. It marks a “That was then, this is now” moment.

Unfortunately, people may be ridiculed by family or friends for mourning the loss of a public figure. They may be reminded, “You didn’t even know them; why do you care so much?” This type of loss is termed disenfranchised grief. When grief is disenfranchised or invalidated, people may feel isolated and forced to find solace online or in public venues where others are mourning the loss as well. That explains why strangers lay sheaves of flowers and other physical tributes at sites such as the Hollywood Boulevard star location of celebrities, or outside the gates of their former homes, or at accident sites. These are ways to give tangible weight to these losses that may be minimized by others.

How to Move Forward Alongside Parasocial Loss

While the immediate feelings of grief over the loss of a celebrity can be just as acute as any loss, it is important to move forward in ways that are emotionally productive, not destructive. By taking action and contributing to the person’s legacy, personal healing can begin. Here are two simple steps to help you process this type of loss:

  1. Engage in collective rituals. Join a digital tribute community that lets you express your own feelings and feel connected to others who felt similarly. And chat with people who shared the admiration for this person that you felt.
  2. Carry the legacy forward. Practice the values that the celebrity modeled, donate resources or time to the philanthropic causes that they promoted, and live out your own life in ways that instill similar values in others.

It’s important to remember that it’s totally natural to cry over the loss of a beloved celebrity. It’s evidence that our capacity for empathy is working exactly as it should be.

item.title: What Is Spiritual Jazz?
item.description:
Spirituality

What Is Spiritual Jazz?

Spirituality is an essential part of existential psychology.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Spiritual jazz creates a container capacious enough to hold tragedy and ecstasy at the same time.
  • John Coltrane’s “A Love Supreme” was the pioneering spiritual jazz album.
  • Music helps people wrestle with emotions and lends solace that other people are exploring similar paths.

I recently stumbled across “Spiritual Jazz Essentials” on Apple Music and it took me back to the 10 years I taught spiritual psychology workshops at the Esalen Institute. During yoga, I would play Alice Coltrane’s “Journey in Satchidananda” because Alice Coltrane espoused Vedanta, a major school of Hindu philosophy that is the origin of the yoga we practice today. What a surprise to discover that an entire genre has spawned from John and Alice Coltrane's devotion!

The Influence of the Coltranes on Spiritual Jazz

This lineage emerged from John Coltrane's albums such as "A Love Supreme," “Meditations,” and “Om” that functioned as prayers, the sound of someone employing a saxophone the way a monk employs a mantra. When John Coltrane died in 1967, his widow Alice, who had been playing piano in his band, continued her husband’s legacy in her own register, turning to Swami Satchidananda and Vedanta for the architecture of her sound. Her 1971 album “Journey in Satchidananda,” recorded on harp and organ and laced with ragas and sitar, is the clearest statement of what spiritual jazz was reaching for: a cosmic universality that embodied every religion inside it at once. Pharoah Sanders erected a similar cathedral in his 1969 album “Karma” with its symphonic “The Creator Has a Master Plan,” which is as close as instrumental music has come to an actual sermon. What united this community was the conviction that a horn or a harp could function as a tool of transcendence and not just as entertainment.

Parallels With Mark Rothko, Kamasi Washington

I think of the painter Mark Rothko whenever I look for a visual analogy because Rothko was doing with color exactly what the Coltranes were doing with musical notes. He believed that people who cried while viewing his paintings were having the same religious experience he had while painting them. There is a Jewish practice of writing “G-d” rather than spelling the name fully, which is rooted in knowing that words cannot fully express the divine. G-d is ineffable and can only be "indicated" or "pointed toward." Rothko, the Coltranes, and the spiritual jazz artists who followed them are all doing exactly that, indicating and pointing through their art and music.

Kamasi Washington is the clearest inheritor of this tradition. “Music is a spiritual thing,” he says. Every song he creates carries that same intense emotional charge, regardless of what genre it gets filed under. He credits his father with bringing Coltrane and Sanders into the house long before he understood what he was hearing. What I love about Washington’s respect for the lineage is what it proves about the work itself: that a saxophonist playing today can draw from the same well that Alice Coltrane and Pharoah Sanders were drawing from 60 years ago.

Therapeutic Potential of Spiritual Jazz

There is a reason people weep in front of certain paintings and certain records without being able to explain why. Kabbalah gave us the vocabulary for it centuries before we had a psychological explanation: The vessels meant to hold the divine light shattered because the light was more than they could contain; the work of a lifetime becomes gathering those scattered sparks back into something whole.

A therapy client who cannot yet sit with the full weight of their own grief or their own quest for meaning and purpose can find something in musicians and artists whose compositions and paintings point toward that wholeness and holiness, a vessel large enough to hold what they cannot yet hold on their own. They find solace knowing that other people are wrestling with the same questions.

What music like John and Alice Coltrane’s does is create a container capacious enough to hold tragedy and ecstasy at the same time. Their sonic explorations can show clients new paths through feelings that once seemed unmanageable and teach them to fit what may feel like overwhelming chaos into a coherent melody.

All of us are vessels gathering those scattered sparks back and learning on a daily basis what we can hold.

The genre of spiritual jazz indicates new paths down that journey.

item.title: The Route to Forgiveness Can Take Surprising Turns
item.description:
Forgiveness

The Route to Forgiveness Can Take Surprising Turns

A new way of thinking about the past can help mend a ripped relationship.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • When someone hurts you, it’s easy to allow your anger and distress to prevent you from granting forgiveness.
  • A new study shows that a mental trick known as counterfactual thinking can help smooth over the hurt.
  • By replaying past events with different endings, your ability to forgive will be that much greater.

Being hurt by someone close to you can cause potentially irreversible harm to the relationship. Claire and Jamie thought nothing could ever break them apart after years of reasonable happiness together. However, Claire was keeping a pretty big secret hidden from Jamie, one that she knew would hurt him. A few months ago, she and a coworker engaged in more than innocent flirtation, coming close to starting an affair. Nothing happened, but she could no longer keep it bottled up inside her. Jamie did not take the news well and said he needed time to think over what to do next.

Forgiveness and Rethinking the Past

The study of forgiveness often involves understanding how people who are hurt can come to manage their distress and move on to reconciliation. According to a new study by Catholic University of Milan’s Mauro Bertolotti and colleagues (2026), there are all kinds of obstacles to restoring a potentially broken relationship. The main obstacle, they propose, is when victims of an offense get stuck using “their own cognitive resources to forgive the perpetrator and move on.” Like Jamie, this can be asking a lot for the brain to process.

One way to move this all along, Bertolotti et al. suggest, is for victims to engage in counterfactual thinking. This is a kind of mental gymnastics in which you relive a past event as if something about that event unfolded differently. It's such a common phenomenon that you may not even realize you’re doing it. Perhaps you dropped one of your prized possessions, and it smashed to smithereens. Putting the event in reverse, you reimagine it with a happier outcome. You almost dropped it, but caught it in time. If only you had done so, you think.

In forgiveness, counterfactual thinking could allow you, the authors propose, to reimagine a situation when you were hurt without the hurtful act having occurred. Jamie remembers talking to Claire, but no bombshell from the past was dropped. This is called a “subtractive” counterfactual. The other type of counterfactual is “additive.” Claire did confess to the peccadillo, but as Jamie thinks about it, she explained the mitigating circumstances. There was a flirtation, it almost led to something serious, but this happened at a time when Claire was under a lot of stress.

The Italian research team proposed that additive counterfactual thinking could provide what’s needed mentally for victims to process a hurtful event and come out on the other side, forgiving the perpetrator. Your mind has something to chew on as it relives the event, allowing you to see things from the perspective of the perpetrator.

Testing the Counterfactual Theory of Forgiveness

Across a series of three studies, Bertolotti and colleagues tested whether their theory of forgiveness would hold up under conditions prompting the two types of counterfactual thinking. In the first study, they gave their undergraduate participants a prompt to recall a time they were upset or hurt by someone close to them. The resulting categories included an argument, being insulted, disloyalty, and distancing (physical and/or emotional). Then the participants generated counterfactual explanations, including both subtractive (“If he had not told me the secret”) and additive (“If he had been honest with me”). These explanations were generated both from the standpoint of victim (as in these examples) or perpetrator (“If I had not told him the secret”).

In the next study, participants reported on a hurtful event but were prompted to generate additive and subtractive counterfactuals, with the outcome measures including willingness to take the other person’s perspective and degree of forgiveness while also controlling for perceived severity and length of time since the event occurred.

With perspective-taking as the mediating factor, the findings supported additive counterfactual thinking’s positive effect on forgiveness. The only problem was that some participants blamed themselves for the hurtful event. To get around this, the authors ran a third study in which they controlled for self-blame. Now the model was intended to apply only to situations where the other person was seen to be at fault. This would become the true test of forgiveness.

With fault ruled out of the equation, additive counterfactual thinking was supported as the route to forgiveness. These findings, suggest the authors, show that “the ways people reflect on and communicate about past events can shape their relationships with others.” What’s more, counterfactual thinking provides those who are wronged with a “unique and expedient tool to explore the path to forgiveness.”

If Jamie were to put this tool to use, it would mean imagining Claire as she was, stressed to the point of giving in to a temporary temptation. Perhaps Claire could have spoken to Jamie about how stressed she was, but perhaps she didn’t feel she could. Although she was clearly at fault, the circumstances leading to the mistake became somewhat more understandable and—most importantly—forgivable.

Finding Your Path to Forgiveness

If you think back on the last time forgiveness was on the table in your closest relationship, what type of thinking did you engage in? Did you honestly try to understand why your partner engaged in this hurtful behavior, or did you either (a) decide never to forgive or (b) push the whole thing out of your mind? The Bertolotti et al. study suggests that by replaying the event in your mind while trying to imagine a different scenario, your mental resources will be much more likely to get you to a point of forgiving the transgression.

At the same time, opening your mind to possible alternate endings to a situation can help you regulate your emotions. The anger, hurt, and distress can subside as you put your more rational thought processes to work.

To sum up, good relationships are made up of people who try to see the world from the perspective of others rather than just from their own viewpoints. If playing out alternative endings helps you reach that point, your relationship and ability to forgive will become that much more fulfilling.

item.title: Longstanding Eating Disorders Are Not Irreversible
item.description:
Eating Disorders

Longstanding Eating Disorders Are Not Irreversible

Why illness duration alone should not define prognosis with eating disorders.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Long illness duration does not mean an eating disorder is irreversible.
  • Intensive, integrated care may improve outcomes in longstanding eating disorder.
  • Healthy weight restoration and continuity of care appear especially important.

For many years, some people with anorexia nervosa and other eating disorders who remained ill despite repeated treatments were described as having a “severe and enduring eating disorder.” The term was intended to identify people with complex and persistent illness. But it also carried a risk: The word enduring can easily be interpreted as permanent.

That matters. If clinicians, patients, or families begin to believe that an eating disorder is unlikely to improve simply because it has lasted many years, therapeutic expectations may gradually shift from recovery toward resignation.

A recent systematic review published in the Journal of Eating Disorders challenges this assumption. The review examined recent studies of adults with severe and longstanding eating disorders and found an important message: The duration of an eating disorder, by itself, does not reliably predict poor treatment outcome.

From “enduring” to “longstanding”

One of the first issues raised by the review is terminology. There is no universally accepted definition of “severe and enduring anorexia nervosa.” Different studies have used arbitrary illness-duration thresholds of three, five, or seven years. Some definitions have also included previous unsuccessful treatments, low weight, or persistent psychopathology. More importantly, people with lived experience have questioned whether the term enduring unintentionally suggests irreversibility.

For this reason, the authors suggest using the expression “longstanding and severe eating disorders” to acknowledge persistence and severity without implying treatment futility, reflecting a broader shift in clinical thinking.

What seems to matter more than illness duration?

Across the studies reviewed, people with longstanding eating disorders were able to make meaningful improvements in weight, eating-disorder psychopathology, general psychological symptoms, functioning, and quality of life. Importantly, illness duration was not a consistent predictor of treatment response.

A more relevant factor was whether patients achieved and maintained a healthier weight, particularly by the time they left intensive treatment. Across several studies of anorexia nervosa, a healthy discharge body mass index (BMI) was more consistently linked to better follow-up outcomes than the duration of illness. This has important clinical implications.

A person who has had anorexia nervosa for 10 or 15 years should not automatically be considered less capable of recovery than someone who has been ill for two or three years. The more useful question may be: “Has this person received a sufficiently intensive, coherent, and continuous treatment?”

Intensive and integrated treatment appears promising

The clearest positive signal in the review came from intensive, integrated treatment pathways. Although the evidence is still largely observational rather than based on randomized controlled trials, the most promising programs shared several features:

  • substantial or full weight restoration
  • specialist psychological treatment
  • multidisciplinary care
  • continuity between inpatient, day-patient, and outpatient treatment

This continuity may be especially important. Several inpatient studies showed substantial improvement during admission, followed by some deterioration after discharge. In other words, helping a patient improve during hospitalization is only part of the challenge. Maintaining that improvement after discharge is equally important.

What the intensive CBT-E studies found

Some of the strongest observational findings in the review came from studies of intensive enhanced cognitive behavior therapy (CBT-E).

In the largest Italian cohort, involving more than 400 adults with anorexia nervosa, more than 80 percent reached a BMI of at least 18.5 kg/m² at the end of intensive treatment, and more than 60 percent met criteria for a full response. More than half maintained full response at follow-up.

A U.K. study comparing different inpatient pathways also reported better long-term outcomes and fewer readmissions among patients receiving an integrated CBT-E pathway than among those receiving less continuous forms of care.

These findings are encouraging, but they should be interpreted cautiously. Because the studies were not randomized, differences in patient selection, treatment preferences, disease severity, or service organization may have influenced the results. Still, the overall pattern is clinically important: Longstanding illness did not prevent substantial improvement.

Outpatient treatment alone may not always be enough

The review also found more limited results for standard outpatient treatment in people with severe and longstanding anorexia nervosa.

In one large U.K. study, patients improved modestly over 12 months, but more than 80 percent of those in the longstanding group eventually required escalation to day or inpatient treatment. This raises an important question: Can remaining for too long in an insufficiently intensive treatment contribute to continued illness?

For some patients, the issue may not be “treatment resistance” but, rather, that the "level of treatment has not matched the severity of the problem."

Recovery and quality of life are not competing goals

Another important message is that weight restoration and quality of life should not be viewed as opposing treatment goals. Malnutrition can affect concentration, emotional regulation, social functioning, physical health, and the ability to engage in psychological treatment. For this reason, nutritional rehabilitation is not merely about changing a number on the scale. It can create the conditions in which broader psychological and social recovery becomes more possible.

Avoiding therapeutic pessimism

The evidence isn't perfect, with most studies on women with anorexia nervosa, limited randomized trials, short follow-ups, and underrepresented diagnoses. However, the review argues that long illness duration doesn't mean irreversibility. A longstanding eating disorder is undoubtedly more complex and needs intensive treatment, but years of illness alone shouldn't dismiss recovery-focused care.

Perhaps the most important shift is from asking: “How long has this person been ill?” to asking: “What treatment has this person received, at what intensity, and with what continuity?”

That change may help replace therapeutic pessimism with a more evidence-informed and recovery-oriented perspective.

item.title: Overlooked Determinants of GLP-1 Usage
item.description:
Health

Overlooked Determinants of GLP-1 Usage

Health behaviors and perceptions play a big role in patient compliance.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • After one year, a high percentage of patients discontinue GLP-1 medications.
  • The WHO has spelled out many behavioral factors involved in medication noncompliance.
  • The solution involves health system and community support on many levels.
Source: Love Employee / iStock

Ever since the Food and Drug Administration's approval of the first GLP-1 in 2005 and the advent of subsequent formulations, consequences of use have been studied extensively. Science has found that GLP-1 use can have an impact on type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, and some cancers. In addition, they have been implicated in helping individuals to curb alcohol addiction.

Despite these glowing reports, it has been reported that only between 27 and 65 percent of individuals are still using these medications after a year. Cost, irregular coverage by insurance companies, availability, and side effects are often cited as the main reasons for quitting.

Unfortunately, often the weight comes back on, and the long-term health benefits are not realized.

It can be easy to pigeonhole the problems of medication compliance with GLP-1s. Too expensive, too many side effects.

It’s important to look at what else may be going on.

Historical Perspective

Even before the first GLP-1 came out in 2005, the World Health Organization (WHO; 2003) came out with a comprehensive look at adherence to long-term therapies. They were concerned about the growing burden of chronic diseases on health and increased health care costs. The gist was that increasing adherence to health interventions would bring about greater health benefits than improving specific medical treatments.

The WHO highlighted five dimensions that can affect adherence.

To summarize:

  • Health system factors—not enough education, follow-up, or support for self-management
  • Low self-esteem, body image issues, or lack of feelings of autonomy over medical issues
  • Lack of supportive community organizations
  • Health beliefs that are not in line with adherence to therapy; limited knowledge about medical issues, especially around chronic diseases
  • Lack of self-management programs aimed at creation and maintenance of healthy habits

Issues With GLP-1s

GLP-1’s represent a significant breakthrough in the treatment of the disease of obesity and many of the chronic diseases that are associated with it, but there are still problems with adherence.

A small qualitative study (Ko et al., 2025) indicated that patients who had been treated for obesity noted the need for improved communication, follow-up, and help with decision-making.

A recent study (DePietro et al., 2026) focused on patient beliefs to examine motivations, barriers, and perceptions around using GLP-1 medications. The study identified several gaps in patients’ perceptions and beliefs around the disease of obesity and nuances involved in GLP-1 use. Most notably:

  1. Participants demonstrated a limited knowledge of GLP-1 side effects and anticipated duration of use. About 75 percent were unsure of the side effects, and 32 percent were not aware that GLP-1s are a long-term therapy.
  2. Many of the participants were not aware of the connections between obesity and several chronic diseases, and the effects GLP-1’s may have on those conditions.
  3. Self-efficacy, or confidence in one’s ability to sustain behaviors leading to weight loss, emerged as a significant factor for people taking GLP-1s or contemplating using them. Many individuals had multiple failed attempts to lose weight before turning to the medication. In fact, 90 percent of individuals in the study contemplating a GLP-1 medication had many unsuccessful previous attempts to lose weight. Lack of success would undermine a person’s sense of control over the process.

A Comprehensive Solution

Underscoring these issues, the WHO recently (2025) issued guidelines for using GLP-1s to treat obesity.

The guidelines are a continuation of the statements from 2003 regarding medication adherence for treatment of chronic diseases.

The WHO refers to obesity as a chronic disease that requires lifetime care. While many of the guidelines are about increasing affordability and access, there is another recommendation that is very clear: “…behavioral and lifestyle changes should be provided as a first step to intensive behavioral therapy to amplify and support optimal health outcomes.”

Doubling down, the WHO specifies structural goal-setting for physical exercise and diet, energy intake restriction, weekly counseling sessions, and routine assessments of progress.

In short, the guidelines include solutions to problems with costs and availability, but they do not neglect the importance of managing the behavioral aspects. Patient education, improvements in health system support, and community engagement are all part of the picture to encourage adherence to GLP-1 medications.

item.title: How Do Self-Forgiveness and Forgiveness of Others Differ?
item.description:
Forgiveness

How Do Self-Forgiveness and Forgiveness of Others Differ?

Self-forgiveness and forgiveness of others have some important distinctions.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Not all forms of forgiveness are the same; this is the case between forgiving others and forgiving oneself.
  • Both forgiving others and the self involve working to offer mercy toward the one who offended.
  • Forgiving the self, however, may need more work because it is often misunderstood regarding what is involved.
Source: Innovatedcaptures / Dreamstime

Over the past three decades, forgiveness has taken its place among the therapeutic approaches to trauma, particularly when a person is treated unjustly. This is because forgiveness is a scientifically supported approach to reducing the resentment that can build in someone who has been unjustly treated (see, for example, Enright & Fitzgibbons, 2015/2024).

Recently, I have been asked: What is the difference between forgiving myself and forgiving others? This post explains how these two processes are not quite the same. Before examining these differences, let us define what we mean by forgiving. Whether we forgive others or ourselves, when we forgive, we are offering goodness, in the form of mercy, toward the one who was not good to the forgiver. This is done without excusing the wrong or abandoning a sense of justice. The common link between the two forms of forgiveness is that the forgiver works on being merciful to others (when they treat us unfairly) or to the self (when we offend ourselves).

We now turn to the differences between the two. We address this with three points.

1. Self-forgiveness can be more easily misunderstood than forgiving others.

In my experience, some people think it is impossible to forgive oneself for at least three reasons. First, some people reason, When I treat myself unjustly, it is hard to discern exactly how unjust I have been because I am biased. In other words, some self-forgivers reason that they have a conflict of interest, so they cannot clearly see whether they behaved badly toward themselves. While it is true that we cannot necessarily discern the exact extent to which we have been unfair to ourselves, this same conflict of interest can descend upon the process of forgiving others. This is the case because, when deeply hurt by others, the resentment can cloud clear thinking with the extreme conclusion that the other person, who was unfair, is a low-down, dirty excuse for a human being. This distorts the reality that this other person is still a person and therefore has inherent worth, even when behaving badly. Therefore, this bias or conflict of interest can occur in either form of forgiveness. A way out of this distortion is to calmly use one’s wisdom and rationality to ask, more than once, How deeply unjust has this action been? This still will not lead to perfection, but it can lead to a more accurate assessment of how unjust the action is, whether it was perpetrated on the self or exclusively on others.

A second misconception occurs when people say this to themselves: Self-forgiveness is impossible because I now become my own judge and defendant. In a court of law, the defendant never becomes the judge. Yet, forgiveness, including self-forgiveness, does not take place in a court, but within the human heart. In other words, placing forgiving inside a court of law is a false analogy. Therefore, those who self-forgive can discern, at least to a degree, the extent of the damage from their unjust actions.

A third misconception emerges from some people with religious beliefs. They conclude: I cannot forgive my own sins; only God can do that. Yet, self-forgiveness and forgiving others are never about forgiving sins. When we forgive others, we have mercy on them; we do not take on the role of the divine. It is the same with self-forgiveness in that we do not forgive our own sins, but instead try to have mercy on ourselves when disappointed with ourselves.

In summary, these arguments against self-forgiveness do not hold up under careful scrutiny.

2. It often is harder to forgive the self than to forgive others.

I say this because of my experience in talking with others who have practiced both kinds of forgiveness. A common statement, usually followed by a sigh, is this: I just can’t forgive myself for what I have done. Even though self-forgiveness can be more challenging than forgiving others, it still is possible with practice and a will to persevere. I usually recommend that people do not start the forgiveness journey by forgiving themselves. Instead, I recommend they first choose a person who has been unjust to them, but not so unjust that they are fuming at the offender. After walking the path of forgiving another, I further recommend then forgiving someone else, again to build up the practice of forgiveness. Once forgivers have confidence in forgiving others, I recommend trying to forgive themselves, especially if they have worked through the misconceptions in point 1 above so confidence in the process is established. It is important to realize here that forgiveness, especially self-forgiveness, can take time, and so it should not be rushed. It takes time to welcome oneself back into the human community when self-loathing has occurred. Seeing one’s own worth as a person, even with all of the imperfections, can take time to sink into the mind and heart.

3. Unlike forgiving others, self-forgiveness often includes going to others and seeking forgiveness from them.

When others treat us badly, we are not the one who needs to seek forgiveness. In contrast, when we self-forgive, we often have been unjust to others. Even when it is not completely obvious that others have been hurt by our actions, those injustices still are present in the background and can be addressed. For example, suppose someone, while intoxicated and alone in the car, is driving way above the speed limit. He crashes his car into a tree and breaks his leg. No one else is hurt, right? Well, he will have to take time off work; his loved ones may have to care for him and help with transportation while he heals. These others may be inconvenienced and have to deal with the trauma of the accident, and an apology to them may be in order.

In summary

Forgiving others and forgiving oneself share the commonality of showing mercy to the one who acted unjustly. Yet, self-forgiveness may need careful explanation regarding why it is legitimate, along with more practice, and then seeking forgiveness from others. The practice of self-forgiveness is important in welcoming the self back into the human community if the person starts to dislike the self because of unjust actions.
