item.title: The 'Here and Now': How Music and Dance Set Us Free
item.description:
Creativity

The 'Here and Now': How Music and Dance Set Us Free

When time and space press in on us, the arts help us find room to breathe.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • The performing arts keep us human in a world where physical time and space are increasingly compromised.
  • We can improve our intentional focus, effort, and energy to hold more mental and physical space open.
  • Engaging with a performance may reveal emotion and energy that needs to be released.

In a modern society of virtual relationships, continuously racing deadlines, and invisible stress, Western classical music and dance provide rich environments for finding ourselves in the present moment.

In my previous post, I explored how conscious listening to Western classical music can sharpen awareness of our relationship to time. Here, I extend that idea to time and space by pairing classical music with classical ballet, which expresses space in a more visceral way than music.

Visible and Invisible Cages

At one time or another, we have had to endure the compression of time and space—financially, spiritually, socially, mentally, emotionally, or geographically. Sometimes we respond by creating our cages in our own imagination. At such moments, we might also imagine our way out of them.

When we get stuck in a cage of our own making, we need some peripheral vision, some help from the collective or higher powers, some revelation through the arts, to find an escape key. If music and dance can help us name the fear—the uncertainty, or the frustration, or the embarrassment—then perhaps we can release emotional expectations and redirect that energy to succeeding or healing or connecting more.

Beyond coping, we look forward to stimulating the brain to desire to communicate with others. To generate curiosity and ask the best questions. The tension and release of music and dance do this instinctively. We can choose to take this opportunity to redefine the moment.

How Music and Dance Set Us Free

In a piece of Western classical music, harmony is the musical element that makes emotional tension and release possible by creating physical instability that then resolves to a stable interval. This natural law of physics is completely compatible with our emotional sensors. A progression of chords will unfold over time. Sometimes we get intentionally disconnected from the home key (the set of pitches that has primary importance), or yield to a new key, and we don’t always know where the music is going to take us.

That sense of uncertainty resonates with real-life experience—living in the present and not knowing what the future will hold. And in dance, this can be expressed through unexpected directional change, interruption of energetic flow, and levels of movement using different heights in space.

In both performance and life, we constantly negotiate between competing and sometimes conflicting thoughts and emotions. The limitless possibilities of what happens next do not have to overwhelm us; they also put us in touch with our sense of free will.

We choose how to respond, how to give ourselves more space to consider options, and how to pace that response in time.

As humans, we have been gifted with the incredible ability to notice simultaneous layers of meaning, to have peripheral vision, and to discern a bigger reality. When we normalize attending to performing arts, we improve this ability.

To Personalize, or Not to Personalize…

Some artists present performance as autobiographical therapy, but this is risky for a big audience with a huge range of comfort levels. Sometimes an unintended result is that we increase the hyper-focus on one painful topic, which is retraumatizing rather than soothing. In somatic bodywork, the work on one pain spot is only helpful when the relief is integrated into the entire body. The same is true on stage.

That integration of different modes is what a live performance offers. The uncomfortable and deeply human experience of “emotional compromise” can be alleviated by stepping out of our personal despair into a collective and attending to the issue through the lens of art rather than the lens of self.

But does the issue have to be shared publicly to be affirmed? Not necessarily. Sometimes the abstract nature of music and dance can give us the cover to try walking out of a cage door in private and without cognitive barriers—even while moving in sync with everyone else in the audience.

Try This Spatial Listening at Home

A dancer’s arm movements (port de bras) are about framing the space between the eyes and the hand. Let your hands slowly explore the space around you, while you focus on the space between your eyes and your hands.

Now put on some peaceful music with a slow melody and focus on the “held spaces” between the start of one note and the start of the next.

Finally, let your hands shape that external space as you breathe to the timing of each note.

Can you experience your agency a little more now?

Performance as an Environment of Consciousness

I use interdisciplinary performance as an environment of consciousness, exploring how the performing arts help us process events and find expressions for our human experience within the limits of mental and physical space. Music helps us become aware of units of time. Dance makes visible the dimensions of space.

As I work with my dancer collaborator Caroline Frank on our upcoming show in New York City, The Compromise of Space, we are exploring the times and spaces in the musical score. Where and how and with what pacing to highlight for the audience a momentary emotional impulse, a mid-range harmonic progression or line of movement, or the overall structure of the piece.

With the performing arts as an essential part of our lifestyle, we strengthen the intentional focus, effort, and energy required to hold more mental and physical space open. With conscious listening skills as training tools to attend to the performance, we become more appreciative of the “here and now.” Schedule a time for daily music listening. Learn to play an instrument. Join a social group that challenges you to engage on a deeper level. Each of these activities improves our ability to find more time and space to savor being alive.

item.title: Why People Keep Making the Same Mistakes
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

Why People Keep Making the Same Mistakes

We keep repeating unhelpful behaviors but CBT can help us change.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Unhelpful behaviors make sense once we understand the thoughts and beliefs behind them.
  • We can usually change unhelpful habits by identifying and responding to unhelpful thoughts.
  • Deep-rooted beliefs can lead to patterns of avoidance, anxiety, or self-sabotage.
  • CBT helps people understand their behavior and and test new ways of thinking and behaving.
Source: nenetus/Adobe Stock

It’s often perplexing to people (and their friends and family) why they continue to engage in behavior that is clearly unhelpful and often in conflict with their important values and goals. Eating or drinking too much, arguing with a partner, continually keeping others waiting, procrastinating on important matters, spending too much time scrolling on their phones — the list could go on and on. In Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT) we help people understand how their behavior is related to their underlying thoughts and beliefs. We know that people’s behavior always makes more sense when you know what they’re thinking.

I’ll describe two clients I recently treated.* One client’s problematic behavior was straightforward and didn’t require a focus on his underlying beliefs, which were, for the most part, realistic, balanced, and helpful. The other client required an exploration of beliefs and assumptions that were associated with a long-standing and entrenched pattern of unhelpful behavior.

When Changing a Habit Is Enough

Mark, a 25-year-old sales associate, was continually late to work. He had a great deal of difficulty getting out of bed in the morning because he often didn’t get into bed until well after midnight.

He liked his job and didn’t want to lose it, but he was having trouble unplugging from the video games he played every evening. “It won’t matter. I’ll just play for 10 more minutes,” he constantly told himself. Ten minutes could then turn into three hours. Feeling sleep deprived when his alarm went off at 6 am, he hit the snooze button. When it went off again, he often told himself, “I’ll just push it one more time, and then I’ll get up. If I skip breakfast, I can still be on time for work.” Sometimes he was. But then he received two written warnings from his manager, and knew that being late one more time could mean losing his job. So he was finally motivated to work on this problem.

I used a number of standard CBT techniques to help Mark change his habits. I had him record the advantages and disadvantages of continuing to play his video game (and continuing to push the snooze button) versus the advantages and disadvantages of not doing that. When he circled the items which felt most important to him, he concluded that it was important to him to change his behavior.

We also explored Mark’s values—the beliefs, principles, and qualities that reflect how we want to live our lives and what we consider important or meaningful. I helped him see that reducing his time playing video games meant he would be living more in alignment with his values of achievement, conscientiousness, and self-control. I also asked him to reflect on how adopting the new behaviors would increase the probability that he’d be able to achieve his aspiration to be successful in business.

We then worked on his unhelpful thinking. He set an alarm on his phone for 10:50 pm that reminded him he might be tempted to keep playing at 11. He set another alarm for 11 pm which reminded him to read the following message:

If I think, It doesn’t matter if I keep playing, remind myself: It’s not true that it doesn’t matter. I don’t want to get fired from this job. If I stop now, I’ll be temporarily disappointed, but I’ll be so glad tomorrow morning when it’s time to get up. I’ll be proud of myself when I break this habit. I want to be stronger than my momentary desire to keep playing.

I asked him to imagine himself reading the message at 11 pm that night and then turning off the video game. We followed the same process for getting up in the morning. We also discussed a reward that Mark would give himself when he had successfully gotten to work on time for an entire month. These few interventions and the anticipation of purchasing a new video game he wanted was enough. He successfully broke his late-night habit. By the end of the month, he had built his confidence and strengthened his resolve. He consistently got to bed on time and kept his job.

When Deeper Beliefs Drive Our Behavior

Many individuals have more deep-rooted unhelpful behaviors and require an additional focus on their underlying beliefs about themselves, others and their world, and the future.

Alyssa often failed to assert herself in situations when doing so would make the most sense. For example, she allowed others to dominate conversations with her. She avoided making reasonable complaints when a product or service was subpar. She didn’t protest when a family member made unreasonable demands. She remained quiet when her boyfriend unfairly criticized her. Why did this pattern show up for her over and over again?

Alyssa may have been naturally somewhat shy and guarded, traits that were strengthened by early negative experiences in her family. Her mother held unreasonably high expectations for her and was critical when Alyssa was unable to meet them. Alyssa often felt hurt by this, taking the criticism to heart, and ruminating about her perceived weaknesses. She often cried and was then teased by her siblings. When her mother yelled at her for not doing her chores well enough, Alyssa would think, “I can’t do anything right.” Over time, Alyssa developed some very strong negative beliefs, especially these two: “I’m incompetent” and “I’m likely to get hurt [emotionally].”

These beliefs became stronger as time went on. Alyssa became vigilant for others’ criticism, sometimes even perceiving neutral evidence as supporting her sense of incompetence, and discounting or disregarding evidence that she could do many things well. This vigilance was an unhelpful coping strategy; she didn’t become fully aware of this tendency until she entered treatment and identified an important assumption: “If I’m on guard with other people, I can protect myself, but if I’m not, I’ll get hurt.”

When Alyssa interpreted a situation as potentially threatening, she engaged in another unhelpful coping strategy: avoidance. She believed, “If I avoid challenges, I’ll be okay, but if I don’t, my incompetence will show” and “If I avoid conflict with others, if I avoid being assertive, if I go along with what other people want, I’ll be okay, but if I don’t, they may criticize me, think less of me, or get mad at me and hurt me.” No wonder Alyssa struggled and continued to behave in unhelpful ways.

When Alyssa recognized that her avoidance led to her not receiving a promotion at work, continually feeling anxious when meeting new people, being manipulated and taken advantage of by so-called friends, and being hesitant to stand up for herself across situations, she sought out CBT. Among many other interventions, I helped her understand how her underlying beliefs affected her interactions with others and led to behavior that wasn’t aligned with her values.

Learning how to respond to her negative thoughts and beliefs allowed her to experiment with approaching situations instead of avoiding them and acting in a reasonably assertive way. When these experiments were successful and did not result in others criticizing her or hurting her, she started to change the unhelpful beliefs that led to avoidance.

A person’s behavior always makes sense once you know what they’re thinking. In Mark’s case, thoughts like “It won’t matter,” led him to continue to play video games long into the night. In Alyssa’s case, her belief that being assertive would result in her being hurt led to her continual avoidance of conflict.

* Names and identifying details have been changed.

item.title: The Danger of Hybrid Abundance
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Danger of Hybrid Abundance

When everything is easy to get, what is worth preserving?

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Abundance of production can quietly become scarcity of appreciation.
  • We can now produce first and decide later, which feels liberating until the pile becomes the problem.
  • The answer is to reintroduce friction consciously where it protects our judgment.
The abundance of text and audio-visuals leads to a new version of inflation. We are in the midst of an A(I)nflation
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

Imagine receiving 50 birthday cards. Until recently, each card carried a small record of effort: someone chose it, found a pen, thought about you, wrote something, located your address, and sent it. The message mattered, but so did the friction around it. Now imagine receiving 50 beautifully composed birthday messages generated in 30 seconds. The prose may be warmer, the jokes sharper, the grammar flawless. Still, the emotional arithmetic has changed. When a polished message can be produced almost without cost, its polish tells us less about how much thought, time, or care went into it.

That small example captures a much larger problem of the generative age. Text, images, music, presentations, video, analysis, and advertising can increasingly be produced by almost anyone at extraordinary speed. This is an expansion of capability worth celebrating. However, it also creates a new kind of inflation. When supply rises dramatically while human attention remains fixed, each additional unit of output has to fight harder to be noticed, remembered, and valued. Abundance of production can quietly become scarcity of appreciation.

Once upon a time, when friction did useful work

For decades, innovation has treated friction as an engineering defect. We wanted faster checkout, instant photographs, one-click ordering, auto-complete, and seamless interfaces. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) extends that logic into the realm of thought and expression: instant ideas, instant prose, instant pictures. Much of this friction deserved to disappear. Yet some forms of difficulty had a hidden function. They forced selection before production. If creating 10 versions of a poster took 10 hours, the second version needed a reason to exist. If rewriting a paragraph was laborious, the writer had an incentive to decide what the paragraph was trying to say. When photographs had to be developed, people took fewer of them and often looked at each one for longer.

Generative AI reverses the sequence. We can now produce first and decide later, which feels liberating until the pile becomes the problem. A 2024 experiment in Science Advances found that access to AI-generated ideas improved the creativity, writing quality, and enjoyment of individual short stories, particularly for less creative writers. At the collective level, however, the AI-assisted stories became more similar to one another. The individual writer gained while the pool of stories lost some diversity. A 2026 Nature Human Behaviour research briefing sharpened that warning: Across roughly 880,000 texts, the spread of AI writing assistance was associated with less varied language, while models preserved meaning and compressed stylistic difference. The danger is not bad content. It is a world saturated with competent content that increasingly resembles everything around it.

The inflation of attention

Economists describe inflation as a decline in the purchasing power of a unit of currency. Something similar can happen to content. If the volume of decent-looking writing, imagery, and audio multiplies while every person still has 24 hours in a day, the average item receives a smaller claim on attention. The bottleneck moves downstream: creation becomes cheap; attention becomes expensive. The World Happiness Report 2026 notes a related shift in digital social life, where concern has grown that the quantity of connections can displace their quality. Content can follow the same trajectory. More can widen access and possibility; beyond a point, more also makes it harder to know what deserves care.

The psychology of ownership adds yet another layer. We tend to cherish things partly because we have participated in their becoming. In a 2026 study of AI-assisted creative writing, people who wrote manually felt more psychological ownership of their stories than those who relied on AI generation. Editing and iterative prompting restored some of that ownership because the person was again making consequential choices. A separate 2026 study on AI-generated art found an equally revealing split: Participants could enjoy AI art aesthetically while assigning it lower economic value. The key mechanism was perceived effort. When human effort and curation were made visible, the valuation penalty diminished. Ease, in other words, does not simply change production costs; it changes the story we tell ourselves about what an object is worth.

When production is cheap, judgment becomes precious

This changes the meaning of creativity. For most of history, the capacity to produce was a limiting factor. Increasingly, the difficult part will be deciding what should be produced, what should survive revision and what should never leave the screen. Which idea deserves another hour? Which photograph merits keeping? Which sentence sounds like you rather than like the statistical centre of millions of previous sentences? Which of 20 plausible options is worth somebody else's scarce attention? These are questions of judgment, and judgment does not scale simply because generation does.

The old productivity reflex can therefore become misleading. Pages written, slides produced, images generated, and posts published once provided rough evidence of effort. AI can inflate those numbers almost without limit. A person can now generate 50 pages without having 50 pages of thought. Quantity remains easy to count, so organizations may continue rewarding it long after it has stopped telling us much. The better barometer may be discernment: what was chosen, what was rejected, what was improved, and why the final object should exist at all. As generic polish becomes abundant, distinctiveness may come increasingly from the parts that resist instant optimization—taste, experience, moral judgment, memory, humor, curiosity, and the willingness to leave a competent suggestion unused.

A practical response: Let’s restore and cherish selective friction

The answer is not to romanticize inconvenience or return to typewriters. It is to reintroduce friction consciously where it protects our judgment:

Before generating, define the purpose in your own words; this prevents the tool from setting the direction simply because it can produce one quickly.

During generation, constrain the number of alternatives, because 20 options often create more noise than insight.

After generation, polish and retouch until it feels like work that is in line with your vision (See step 1) and values: cut, reorder, challenge, rewrite, and add what the system could not know. Finally, raise the threshold for release.

Before sending, posting, or publishing, ask whether the output would still feel worth sharing if it had taken a day rather than a minute to produce.

Generative AI is solving an old problem with astonishing speed: the difficulty of making things. It leaves us with a more demanding human task. We have to decide what deserves attention before abundance dulls our capacity to care. The scarcest resource of the hybrid economy is not ideas, images, or words, but the human ability to choose and appreciate what is worth keeping.

item.title: The Stress of Legal Immigration Into the United States
item.description:
Stress

The Stress of Legal Immigration Into the United States

How to reduce anxiety for immigrants.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows immigrants—particularly refugees and asylum seekers—have elevated risk for PTSD and depression.
  • Social networks are essential to humans, even the most individualistic among us.
  • Policymakers should focus on predictability and humanity in immigration processes.
Source: Frank Kastle / Unsplash

Many legal immigrants experience psychological stress throughout the immigration process. Natural disasters, political instability, religious intolerance, economic hardships, civil wars, and other unfavorable conditions often create intense pre-migration stress in the country of origin (Morey et al., 2018). The shift in residence also entails considerable stress associated with logistics and travel. And then, once immigrants have arrived in the host country, there are more psychological stresses due to changes in social status and disruption of social networks. In the United States, there is another layer of stress because of how our society treats immigrants.

How might we transform the United States legal immigration process so that immigrants don’t face so much psychological stress? To answer this question, I reached out to Andrew Rasmussen, professor of psychology and head of the Culture, Migration, and Community research group at Fordham University. His research focuses primarily on the psychosocial needs and assessment of displaced populations. I asked Rasmussen what I think are the five most important questions that policymakers and community leaders should be asking.

JP: Why is it important for policymakers and community leaders to focus on the psychological stress of individuals immigrating to the United States?

AR: I think this is a central question facing our nation in its 250th year. The current administration's implicit answer seems to be: "We should study immigrants' psychological stress so we can increase it to deter them." But that's probably not the spirit of your question. Studies show immigrants make for healthy, happy workers who work harder and longer in labor-starved industries. Immigrants and their children win a disproportionate share of scientific and literary prizes. While some stress is needed to unlock excellence, the stress of leaving home for a new life is already enough—no need for added stress upon arrival. Given immigrants' outsized contributions, policymakers should focus on predictability and humanity in immigration processes, for the nation's own good.

Maybe it's the America 250 mood, but this touches something I underappreciated before working with immigrants: the rule of law. Through three decades of research and practice, it has come up again and again. Sure, America’s economy, democracy, and egalitarian spirit matter, but underlying them is the rule of law—it sets the ground rules for how people are to be treated, subverting stress that comes from not knowing what might come next. It's valued for keeping us safe, but also for protecting us when those meant to keep us safe do something wrong. When officials twist the law with brute force against immigrants, they're breaking one of our most important national promises.

JP: How do disruptions in social networks impact the psychological stress of immigrants?

Social networks are essential to humans, even the most individualistic among us. In conservation of resources theory (Hobfoll, 1989), social networks are an essential resource for psychological well-being in themselves, but they're also crucial for accessing other resources—information, work, loving relationships. For immigrants from collectivist cultures, social networks matter even more. So, disruptions have impacts.

But how disruptions occur matters greatly. Planned disruptions, common among immigrants, cause some stress but are generally adapted to with few long-term detriments—sometimes even benefiting well-being. For example, immigrant parents who precede their children to establish themselves financially report feeling safer in their neighborhoods than those who migrate with their children; this reduces their overly strict parental monitoring (Rasmussen et al., 2018).

Unplanned disruptions are another story. Family members separated by war lose not only each other emotionally but material resources, too. Family members separated by immigration policies live in limbo, not knowing when they'll regain all that family provides, compounded by the grief of sudden separation.

So disruptions in social networks matter greatly—but how they happen is important.

JP: What are the psychosocial needs of immigrants that we should be thinking about?

AR: By "we," I presume you mean mental health professionals. Research shows some immigrants—particularly refugees and asylum seekers—have elevated risk for PTSD and depression, and face many lower-level daily hassles that impact their well-being as well. But epidemiological research shows the medical "healthy immigrant effect"—lower disease risk than comparable native-born populations—applies to mental health, too.

What to make of this? I tell students: First, expect immigrants to be generally resilient—they had the resources to leave home and make it here. Second, check for adversity threatening that resilience. To policymakers, I'd answer: Fund research again! And remember that immigrants’ resilience is exactly why you want them here.

JP: How does the immigration court experience impact psychological stressors of individuals that are immigrating to the United States?

AR: Many people in immigration court have a deportation order and believe they have some claim that invalidates that order (e.g., asylum). So, if you're in immigration court, you're already under a lot of stress, but also holding out some hope of staying.

Any court appearance is stressful, but many immigrants find U.S. procedures counterintuitive. Most countries use a "fact-finding" approach seeking the whole truth; the U.S. adversarial approach has each side arguing until the judge decides which side wins. Many immigrants naively think their honesty about being good people, admitting mistakes, and all, will be enough. So, the process itself is confusing—and therefore stressful.

Preparation can be dehumanizing. Attorneys need clients to relate their claims—often traumatic—clearly and consistently, which means practicing their testimony. For most, talking to attorneys is the first time they've spoken of these events, and, as we know, retelling trauma is hard. Memory being what it is, peripheral details can get omitted—which plays poorly in court—so clients must rehearse their testimony again and again. Many think their attorneys are being cruel.

This evinces an unrealistic assumption of immigration court: that any inconsistency in a trauma narrative means the whole thing is a lie. Psychologists know memory isn't a carbon copy of events, and details shift slightly each time we recall them. Trauma adds a twist—core memories tend to be remembered well, but peripheral details are often fuzzy—and the make-or-break recall setting of the courtroom doesn’t help.

JP: How can we measure improvements to the immigration process and experience with respect to addressing psychological stress?

AR: Are you asking what should change? First, we'd need to value reducing psychological stress in the immigration process. Some fixes are simple: Stop the cruelty and dehumanization; stop flooding immigrant communities with agents to spread fear. I realize that won't happen soon.

Other fixes aren't simple: If we accept that borders can't be fully open, how do we build an enforcement system that follows the law and treats people humanely? I don’t think we've ever actually had that system. Unfortunately, we can't even have that conversation under the current regime in which cruelty toward immigrants is the primary policy tool.

item.title: Seagulls Versus Googly Eyes
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Seagulls Versus Googly Eyes

Googly eyes may be a secret weapon to stop animals from stealing your lunch.

Posted September 21, 2026

Key points
  • If you eat lunch at the park or by the ocean, some enterprising animal may steal your lunch.
  • People have used a variety of noises, smells, and visual stimuli to keep animals away.
  • Humans and other animals track eye gaze for a variety of reason; watching someone is often seen as a threat.
  • Googly eyes on your lunch box may help, slowing down the lunch thieves if you look away for a moment.

Have you ever had your lunch stolen by a gull or some other bird? In the battle to save your lunch, scientists may have discovered a secret weapon: googly eyes.

Keeping Animals Away

People have used a variety of noises, smells, and visual stimuli to keep animals away (Kelley et al., 2026). Maybe you’ve sprayed your roses with coyote spray to keep the deer away — we’ve used these products, but then we don’t like the way the roses smell. Around our community, farmers have a variety of noises and visual displays they use to keep the birds (especially starlings) away from the blueberries as they ripen.

A Stolen Lunch in the Park

Eating lunch at the park or by the ocean has risks. The risk is that if you turn your back, some enterprising animal may steal your lunch. In the Pacific Northwest, where I live, we deal with squirrels, crows, and other birds in our parks. If you go down by the shore or marina, you have to watch for the gulls. Every one of them has learned to beg or steal food from humans. Sometimes these ingenious creatures wait until we toss the leftovers in the trash. Sometimes they beg for food, and we oblige by tossing a chip or a piece of bread. But sometimes they grab the whole sandwich or bag of chips if we turn away or leave our lunch unattended for a moment. For many animals, you and I can be a reliable source of snacks.

But maybe you don’t want to share your lunch with the seagulls (for the purists, I know that the correct term is gulls, not seagulls). Then you have to keep your lunch close at hand.

And it helps to stare down the lunch thieves.

Eye Gaze Matters: What Are You Looking At?

Humans track eye gaze for a variety of reasons. We can judge what someone is interested in by noting where they are looking. If they are looking at us, we recognize that they are interested in us. Even young children use eye gaze to understand what someone else is thinking about (see my post "Mind-Reading Children"). Of course, we also overestimate how much people are looking at us and how aware other people are of what we look like, what we’re wearing, or if we’ve gotten a haircut (read about the spotlight effect).

Animals and Eye Gaze

Non-human animals also track your eye gaze to some extent. No one likes being stared at. Many animals see direct eye contact as a form of aggression. If animals think that a predator is looking at them, they will treat it as a risk and work to escape. With animals in the same species, looking at one another can often be a form of dominance display (humans also have staring contests). Some have argued that animals have many color patterns and displays that look like eyes because eye gaze is seen as both a threat and a show of dominance.

Googly Eyes and Seagulls

All of this leads us to the googly eyes.

In a fun recent study, Laura Kelley and colleagues (2025) investigated whether various types of eyes on a lunch box would deter seagulls. In one study, they used a plain white take-out food box and compared that to the same box with googly eyes attached. They placed these two different food boxes near a herring gull. The gulls were much more likely to peck at the box without the googly eyes. The googly eyes protected the food!

In another study, they first tossed small pieces of bread to a herring gull before presenting either the plain box or the box with googly eyes. This is clearly entrapment. They had just fed the gull, and then they checked how long before the gull went after the food box when left alone. The gulls went after the plain box almost immediately. They waited longer for the box with googly eyes, and about half never went after the food box with googly eyes.

They also tried boxes with drawings of eyes instead of googly eyes. The drawings also deterred gulls from stealing the lunch, but drawings may not be as effective as googly eyes.

Will Googly Eyes Save Your Lunch?

Should you try this at home or in the park? First, there’s no guarantee this will work with other species. I make no promise that googly eyes would slow down a raven in the Pacific Northwest. I’m not risking my lunch to test a raven — those birds are smart. Second, the googly eyes deterred the herring gulls when that was the only decoration on an otherwise plain white box. With a more complex lunch box, I doubt the googly eyes will stand out as much. Finally, googly eyes may slow down or convince a gull to go after a different lunch box. But if you leave that lunch there long enough, I doubt even googly eyes will stop a gull.

But for a short-term deterrent? Googly eyes may help. They may slow down the lunch thieves long enough that you could look away for a moment without losing your lunch.
